papers.title: Thermostable Carbohydrate-Active Enzymes for High-Temperature Biomass Conversion: From Molecular Design to Process Integration.
papers.abstract: High-temperature processing of carbohydrate-rich biomass, including starch liquefaction and lignocellulose saccharification, can improve sugar yields, reduce contamination risks, and facilitate integration with thermochemical pretreatments. However, the operational stability of native carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) at 60-90 °C remains a major bottleneck for efficient and economically viable biorefineries, and existing reviews rarely integrate multiscale molecular mechanisms with process-relevant engineering strategies. This review systematically examines the multiscale basis of thermost
papers.summary: This review examines the molecular and structural basis of thermostability in carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) used for high-temperature biomass conversion, such as starch liquefaction and lignocellulose saccharification at 60-90 °C. It connects protein-level design strategies (e.g., stabilizing mutations, rigidification) with process-integration considerations for biorefineries, arguing that native enzymes are a bottleneck for economically viable high-temperature processing. The work aims to bridge multiscale molecular mechanisms with engineering strategies rarely integrated in prior reviews.

papers.title: Syndirella: synthesis-directed fragment elaboration enables extensive and cost-effective binding site exploration beyond catalog compounds.
papers.abstract: Fragment screens provide an information-rich starting point for designing derivative compounds in structure-based drug discovery. However, derivatives in the fragment-to-hit stage are typically designed from only one or a few fragments, risking premature convergence on an unproductive series and dramatically limiting exploration of the binding site's interaction opportunities. This is avoidable by exploring a broad, chemically diverse set of scaffolds and elaborations spanning interactions revealed across many fragments, as well as those not yet observed. Conventional catalog procurement makes
papers.summary: Syndirella is a computational tool that designs derivative compounds from multiple fragment screening hits rather than just one or a few, enabling broader exploration of a binding site's interaction opportunities. By directing synthesis toward diverse scaffolds and elaborations, it helps avoid premature convergence on unproductive chemical series and makes fragment-to-hit optimization more cost-effective than relying on catalog compounds alone.

papers.title: Structure-Based Engineering for PTPσ-Targeted Therapeutic Development.
papers.abstract: Protein tyrosine phosphatase sigma (PTPσ) is a member of the leukocyte common antigen-related (LAR) family of receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatases. Its architecture integrates an extracellular proteoglycan-sensing region, a single-pass transmembrane helix, and tandem intracellular phosphatase domains. In neural injury, inhibition of PTPσ signaling can relieve chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan (CSPG)-mediated restriction of axonal growth and plasticity. In rheumatoid arthritis (RA), by contrast, restoration of PTPσ activity in fibroblast-like synoviocytes can suppress pathogenic migration
papers.summary: This review discusses structure-based engineering strategies for targeting PTPσ, a receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatase involved in neural injury and rheumatoid arthritis. The authors describe PTPσ's domain architecture—extracellular proteoglycan-sensing region, transmembrane helix, and tandem intracellular phosphatase domains—and how modulating its activity could promote axonal growth after neural injury or suppress pathogenic synoviocyte migration in RA. The work highlights how structural understanding can guide therapeutic development for this dual-role target.

papers.title: Plasma Carrier Proteins as Supramolecular Nanovectors for Cancer Therapy: The Trojan Horse Approach.
papers.abstract: Conventional chemotherapeutics often suffer from poor aqueous solubility, short circulation half-lives, lack of tumor selectivity, and present dose-limiting systemic toxicity. This perspective examines the Trojan Horse Approach (THA), in which plasma carrier proteins (PCPs) are exploited as discrete, non-covalent supramolecular hosts for chemotherapeutic agents, and discusses its potential to overcome the limitations of both free drugs and conventional protein nanoparticles. Two principal strategies for assembling ex vivo drug-protein complexes are discussed: (i) molecular recognition, in whic
papers.summary: This perspective article discusses the Trojan Horse Approach, which uses plasma carrier proteins (PCPs) as non-covalent supramolecular hosts to deliver chemotherapeutic drugs. It outlines two main strategies for assembling drug-protein complexes ex vivo—molecular recognition and covalent conjugation—and argues this approach can overcome limitations of free drugs and conventional protein nanoparticles, such as poor solubility, short half-life, and lack of tumor selectivity.

papers.title: Solution characterization of TrhW, a type 4 secretion system regulatory protein from the R27 plasmid.
papers.abstract: Type IV secretion systems (T4SSs) are multiprotein nanomachines that mediate conjugative DNA transfer and contribute to the dissemination of antimicrobial resistance genes. The IncHI1 plasmid R27 encodes TrhW, a periplasmic T4SS-associated protein homologous to the F-plasmid proteins TraW and TrbC, which are expressed as separate polypeptides in many F-like systems but are fused into a single protein in IncHI1 plasmids. Despite its proposed role in conjugation, the structural organization of TrhW has remained unknown. Here, we employed complementary computational and solution-based biophysical
papers.summary: This study characterizes TrhW, a periplasmic protein from the IncHI1 plasmid R27 that is part of a type IV secretion system involved in conjugative DNA transfer and antibiotic resistance spread. TrhW is unusual because it fuses two proteins (TraW and TrbC) that are separate in other F-like systems, and the authors use computational and biophysical methods to determine its structural organization in solution. The work provides the first structural insight into this fused T4SS protein, which may inform efforts to block plasmid conjugation.

papers.title: Unique features of EIGHT fold-Proteins with the most complex 83 knotted topology.
papers.abstract: Herein, we present three crystal structures of the most complex knotted protein to date, an [Formula: see text] knot with eight crossings, which belongs to a clasp knot family. The fold of this protein is also unique, and we call it the EIGHT fold (Extraordinarily Intricate Globular Helical Tangled fold). The [Formula: see text] knot is found only in a certain group of bacteria, where it is strictly conserved, despite sequence identities as low as 10%. The [Formula: see text] structure shows a high level of internal symmetry, with structurally analogous halves. It is possible that the EIGHT fo
papers.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
papers.summary: The authors report three crystal structures of the most complex protein knot known to date—an eight-crossing knot—which they term the EIGHT fold. This extraordinarily intricate knotted topology is strictly conserved in a specific group of bacteria despite sequence identities as low as 10%, and the structure displays internal symmetry with structurally analogous halves.

papers.title: CCAN forms the spherical shell-like structure in interphase kinetochores.
papers.abstract: The kinetochore is an essential structure for the faithful chromosome segregation during mitosis. The 16-protein complex known as the constitutive centromere-associated network (CCAN) localizes the centromere throughout the cell cycle and forms the basis of the kinetochore. Although cryo-electron microscopy has provided a structural model of an individual CCAN unit, how multiple CCAN units are organized within cells remains unclear. Here, using in silico and in vivo analyses, we demonstrate that multiple CCAN units form a spherical shell-like structure in interphase DT40 kinetochores. CENP-T a
papers.summary: Using computational modeling combined with in vivo experiments in DT40 cells, the authors show that multiple copies of the 16-protein CCAN complex assemble into a spherical shell-like architecture at interphase centromeres/kinetochores. This extends prior cryo-EM structures of single CCAN units to a higher-order cellular organization, with CENP-T playing a key role in the assembly.

papers.title: Bioprocessing of Talaromyces purpurogenus for production of dihydromonascorubrin with a powerful antioxidant and antimicrobial activities integrated with the network-guided target prediction and molecular docking analyses.
papers.abstract: The antibiotic resistance of pathogenic microorganisms due to the irresponsible use in healthcare and agricultural practices is one of the global threats for the human, especially immune-compromised patients. Thus, searching for a novel compounds from fungi with unique affinity to combat the drug-resistant microorganisms was the objective. Talaromyces purpurogenus # PZ292970.1, an endophyte of palm tree Elaeis guineensis, has the highest productivity of azaphilone pigment (25.5 AU410/ml), with a strong activity against E. coli (MIC value 6.8 µg/ml), S. aureus and C. albicans (MIC value 12.5 µg
papers.summary: This study optimized bioprocessing of the fungal endophyte Talaromyces purpurogenus to produce the azaphilone pigment dihydromonascorubrin, which showed strong antioxidant and antimicrobial activity against E. coli, S. aureus, and C. albicans. The authors combined network-guided target prediction and molecular docking to propose mechanisms for the compound's bioactivity.

papers.title: Astragali Radix-Curcumae Rhizoma synergistically potentiates 5-fluorouracil antitumor efficacy in colorectal cancer by disrupting DNA repair-cell cycle coordination.
papers.abstract: Astragali Radix (HQ) and Curcumae Rhizoma (EZ), collectively termed AC, are commonly used as an herb pair in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) for colorectal cancer (CRC). Although AC has been used as an adjuvant to chemotherapy, the molecular basis by which it enhances the efficacy of 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) remains incompletely defined.
papers.summary: This study investigates how a traditional Chinese medicine herb pair (Astragali Radix and Curcumae Rhizoma, 'AC') enhances the antitumor effects of the chemotherapy drug 5-fluorouracil in colorectal cancer. The authors propose that AC works by disrupting the coordination between DNA repair and cell cycle progression, making cancer cells more vulnerable to 5-FU. The work provides a molecular rationale for using this herbal combination as a chemotherapy adjuvant.

papers.title: Competition-dominated microbial interactions and adaptive mutations enhance synthetic denitrifying community functions.
papers.abstract: Understanding how interspecific interactions shape ecosystem functioning is a fundamental and longstanding question in ecology, especially along an evolutionary trajectory. Here, we used experimental evolution to evaluate how microbial interactions and adaptive mutations shaped community-level functions in synthetic denitrifying communities (SDCs) along a species richness gradient (one, two, and six species). Our results showed that competitive microbial interactions were observed and significantly (P < 0.05) enhanced denitrification rates in the six-species SDCs during experimental evolution.
papers.summary: This study used experimental evolution to track how interactions among denitrifying bacteria affect community function across a species-richness gradient. Competition dominated the interactions and significantly boosted denitrification rates in six-species synthetic communities, with adaptive mutations contributing to the functional gains. The work links ecological interactions and evolution to ecosystem-level function.

papers.title: Xanthine oxidase inhibitory evaluation of prenylated flavonoids from peanut (Arachis hypogaea L.) shells: in vitro and in silico molecular docking studies.
papers.abstract: Sustainable agriculture has become a crucial priority because the improper management of agricultural waste currently contributes to greenhouse gas emissions, as well as soil and air pollution. The shells of Arachis hypogaea L., which is commonly discarded as an agricultural by-product, have been reported to contain various secondary metabolites, including flavonoids, stilbenes, triterpenoids, etc. This work led to the isolation of two new prenylated flavonoids, arachisflavones A (1) and B (2), together with five prenylated flavones (3-7), two prenylated chalcones (8-9), and three prenylated f
papers.summary: This study isolated two new prenylated flavonoids (arachisflavones A and B) along with several known prenylated flavones and chalcones from peanut shells, an agricultural by-product. The compounds were tested for xanthine oxidase inhibition in vitro and docked computationally to explore binding, identifying peanut shell flavonoids as potential natural xanthine oxidase inhibitors relevant to gout or oxidative stress.

papers.title: Rational design and synthesis of furan-based Schiff base quinazolin-4-amine hybrids: spectral elucidation, molecular docking, DFT studies, and in silico ADMET-antioxidant study.
papers.abstract: In this work, a new series of furan-based quinazoline-4-amine hydrazone (Schiff base) derivatives (4a-h) was rationally designed and synthesized in good yields (84-90%) through a multistep route involving nucleophilic aromatic substitution, Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling, and hydrazone/Schiff base condensation reactions. The synthesized compounds were characterized by FT-IR, 1H NMR, 13C NMR, and ESI-mass spectrometry, which confirmed the proposed structures. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed to optimize the molecular geometries and to derive frontier molecular orbital
papers.summary: The authors synthesized a series of eight furan-based quinazoline-4-amine Schiff base hybrids using a multistep route (nucleophilic aromatic substitution, Suzuki coupling, and hydrazone condensation) and confirmed their structures by IR, NMR, and mass spectrometry. DFT calculations were used to optimize geometries and analyze frontier molecular orbitals, and the compounds were evaluated in silico via molecular docking and ADMET-antioxidant predictions. The work is a medicinal chemistry design/synthesis study with computational characterization rather than experimental biological validation.

papers.title: NU-1025 modulates immunogenic cell death in bladder cancer: A multi-omics insight.
papers.abstract: Immune checkpoint blockade has shown limited efficacy in bladder cancer, underscoring the need for therapeutic strategies that enhance tumor immunogenicity. Immunogenic cell death (ICD) can stimulate adaptive immunity and remodel the tumor microenvironment, yet its comprehensive landscape and druggable potential in bladder cancer remain unexplored. Here, we performed integrative bioinformatics analysis of transcriptomic data from TCGA and GEO bladder cancer cohorts to characterize ICD-associated subtypes, construct a prognostic risk model, and analyze immune infiltration. Connectivity Map (CMa
papers.summary: This study used integrative bioinformatics on TCGA and GEO bladder cancer transcriptomes to characterize immunogenic cell death (ICD)-associated subtypes, build a prognostic risk model, and profile immune infiltration. The authors then used Connectivity Map analysis to identify NU-1025 as a compound that modulates ICD in bladder cancer. The work is exploratory and computational, proposing a candidate drug and risk model that require experimental validation.

papers.title: CYP1B1 is a potential target of kaempferol in renal fibrosis: a multi‑omics and single‑cell transcriptomics study.
papers.abstract: Renal fibrosis (RF) is a progressive and irreversible pathological process for which effective treatments are limited. This study explores the molecular targets and mechanisms through which kaempferol (Kae) ameliorates RF, with particular emphasis on cytochrome P450 1B1 (CYP1B1).
papers.summary: This study uses multi-omics and single-cell transcriptomics to identify CYP1B1 as a potential molecular target through which the flavonoid kaempferol ameliorates renal fibrosis. The work nominates a specific cytochrome P450 enzyme as a therapeutic node in a progressive, treatment-limited kidney disease.

papers.title: A gut microbiota-metabolite-host gene score for subtyping and predicting the treatment response in rheumatoid arthritis: integrative analysis with in silico knockout validation.
papers.abstract: The pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) involves a complex interplay between immune dysregulation and metabolic disturbance, with the gut microbiota and its metabolites playing pivotal roles. However, integrated biomarkers based on the "gut microbiota-metabolite-host gene" regulatory axis that can quantify its impact on RA stratification and therapeutic response are lacking.
papers.summary: This study constructs an integrated score combining gut microbiota composition, microbial metabolites, and host gene expression to subtype rheumatoid arthritis patients and predict their response to treatment. The authors validate key microbial-metabolite-host gene relationships using in silico knockout simulations. The resulting score stratifies RA patients into distinct subtypes with differing therapeutic outcomes.

papers.title: Cross-linking mass spectrometry guided structure prediction of disordered Encephalitozoon hellem proteins.
papers.abstract: Microsporidia such as Encephalitozoon hellem are obligate intracellular human parasites that remain genetically intractable, limiting the functional characterization of their proteomes. Experimental structural studies are challenging, as many proteins in microsporidia comprise a large percentage of disordered regions. Computational structural studies based on homology-based modeling and the use of deep-learning algorithms for microsporidian proteins also remain limited because most have little to no sequence similarity to proteins with solved structures. To address these limitations, we develo
papers.summary: The authors combine cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) with computational structure prediction to model disordered proteins from the microsporidian parasite Encephalitozoon hellem, which lacks tractable experimental and homology-based approaches. XL-MS-derived distance restraints guide deep-learning predictions, enabling structural characterization of proteins that are largely disordered and have few solved homologs. This provides a workflow for studying genetically intractable organisms with highly disordered proteomes.

papers.title: A water-pinning hot spot drives templated tau aggregation.
papers.abstract: Tau assembles into fibrillar aggregates that are pathological hallmarks of a group of neurodegenerative diseases collectively called tauopathies. Templated aggregation of naïve tau to seeding-competent fibrils that proceed from cell to cell is a key driver of prion-like progression of tauopathies. This study tests the hypothesis that tau, an intrinsically disordered protein, achieves in-register stacking to form seed-competent fibrils by a pinning action of tau to each other and/or the seed surface via a single dominant hotspot to avoid mismatch in tau stacking to fibrils. Structured solvation
papers.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
papers.summary: This study investigates how tau, an intrinsically disordered protein, forms seed-competent fibrils capable of templated aggregation and cell-to-cell spread in tauopathies. The authors propose that a single dominant water-pinning hotspot enables in-register stacking of tau molecules onto fibril seeds, preventing mismatched incorporation. The work provides mechanistic insight into the prion-like propagation of tau pathology.

papers.title: Mononuclear Mg(ii) and Ca(ii) metallocarboxylates of N-phthaloyl-γ-aminobutyric acid: synthesis, characterization, ds-DNA binding, preliminary anticancer evaluation against MDA-MB-231 cells, and computational studies.
papers.abstract: This study reports the synthesis of neurotransmitter-inspired, biolabile mononuclear Mg(ii)/(NY1) and Ca(ii)/(NY2) metallocarboxylates of N-phthaloyl-γ-aminobutyric acid ligand (NPGABA), motivated by the growing relevance of metallocarboxylates in addressing essential metal-ion deficiencies. Extensive spectral (i.e. IR, UV-vis, 1H-NMR, 13C-NMR, AAS, and ICP-AES) and analytical (SEM, micro-analysis and thermal gravimetric analysis) techniques were used to characterize and confirm the formation of the ligand and its metal carboxylate complexes. The complexes were confirmed to have the formulas [
papers.summary: This paper reports the synthesis and characterization of two new mononuclear metal complexes (Mg(II) and Ca(II)) formed with a neurotransmitter-inspired ligand, N-phthaloyl-γ-aminobutyric acid. The authors characterize the compounds spectroscopically and analytically, show they bind double-stranded DNA, and report preliminary anticancer activity against MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells, supported by computational docking/studies. The work is exploratory and early-stage, focused on a narrow class of coordination compounds.

papers.title: Hydrophobic (deep) eutectic solvents: from characterization and modeling to rational design and applications.
papers.abstract: (Deep) eutectic solvents (DESs) have emerged as versatile designer solvents because of their simple preparation, broad compositional flexibility, and highly tunable physicochemical properties. Hydrophobic (deep) eutectic solvents (HDESs), first reported in 2015, further extend the potential of eutectic solvents to aqueous and multiphase systems by exhibiting limited affinity toward water. This feature has generated growing interest in HDESs for separation, resource recovery, pollutant removal, gas capture, and reaction processes. Despite their rapid development, HDES research remains relativel
papers.summary: This review surveys hydrophobic deep eutectic solvents (HDESs), a class of designer solvents first reported in 2015 that have limited affinity for water and thus work well in aqueous and multiphase systems. It covers their characterization, modeling, rational design, and applications in separation, resource recovery, pollutant removal, gas capture, and reaction processes, while noting that the field is still relatively immature.

papers.title: Mapping Ligand-Induced Conformational Changes during the Enzymatic Cycle of Human Geranylgeranyl Diphosphate Synthase.
papers.abstract: Geranylgeranyl diphosphate synthase (GGDPS) catalyzes the condensation reaction between two isoprenoid substrates: farnesyl diphosphate (FDP) and isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP), to form geranylgeranyl diphosphate (GGDP). Due to the flexible nature of the GGDPS active site and its capacity to bind multiple ligands during the reaction coordinate, understanding the structural changes that enable it to accommodate different ligands and catalyze the reaction is essential. While structures exist of substrate and product-bound GGDPS, a lack of high-resolution apo or Mg2+-only structures prevents com
papers.summary: This study maps the conformational changes that human geranylgeranyl diphosphate synthase (GGDPS) undergoes as it binds substrates and cofactors during its catalytic cycle. By obtaining high-resolution structures of the apo and Mg2+-bound states, the authors fill a gap in structural knowledge and reveal how active-site flexibility enables the enzyme to accommodate different ligands. These findings clarify the structural basis for GGDPS catalysis and may inform inhibitor design.

papers.title: Substrate-bound structures of yeast ALA synthase reveal protein dynamics initiating heme biosynthesis.
papers.abstract: Heme is an essential prosthetic group involved in multiple biological processes in nearly all organisms. Heme biosynthesis is initiated by the pyridoxal 5'-phosphate-dependent enzyme aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS). Mutations in ALAS cause multiple hematological diseases. Despite sharing approximately 70% sequence similarity, ALAS homologs exhibit distinct expression and regulatory mechanisms. However, the molecular basis for their functional divergence remains poorly understood. Here, we used x-ray crystallography and molecular dynamics simulations to elucidate the structure and dynamics
papers.summary: This study reports X-ray crystal structures of yeast aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS) bound to its substrate, combined with molecular dynamics simulations, to reveal how protein dynamics initiate heme biosynthesis. The work provides structural insight into the first committed step of heme production and helps explain how ALAS homologs with ~70% sequence similarity diverge functionally. These findings may inform understanding of ALAS mutations that cause hematological diseases.

papers.title: Harnessing the ubiquitin-proteasome system: advances and challenges of PROTACs in breast cancer.
papers.abstract: Breast cancer is one of the most significant health issues in the world, and resistance to treatment and a lack of targets that can be addressed with drugs limit the effectiveness of the existing treatment options. The development of proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) has shifted the concept of occupancy-based inhibition toward event-based targeted protein degradation. Avoiding ubiquitin-proteasome hijacking, PROTACs target disease-relevant proteins to E3 ligases, allowing them to be catalytically degraded, thereby eliminating formerly undruggable or resistant targets. Their modular desi
papers.summary: This review examines PROTACs (proteolysis-targeting chimeras) as an emerging therapeutic strategy for breast cancer, shifting from traditional occupancy-based inhibition to event-based targeted protein degradation. PROTACs recruit disease-relevant proteins to E3 ligases for catalytic degradation, potentially addressing previously undruggable or treatment-resistant targets. The authors discuss advances and remaining challenges in applying this approach to breast cancer.

papers.title: Phospholipase Fluorogenic Probes and Molecular Determinants of Cyclic Guanosine Monophosphate-Adenosine Monophosphate Binding to Cyclic Oligonucleotide-Based Antiphage Signaling System CapV.
papers.abstract: Cyclic oligonucleotide-based antiphage signaling systems (CBASS) protect bacteria from bacteriophage infection by producing cyclic nucleotide second messengers that activate downstream effector proteins. Cyclic guanosine monophosphate-adenosine monophosphate (cGAMP)-activated phospholipase in Vibrio (CapV) is a prevalent CBASS effector whose activity is commonly monitored using the commercially available fluorogenic substrate resorufin butyrate; however, this probe is hydrolyzed by both basal and activated CapV, limiting its usefulness in CapV-related studies. Here, we report the rational desi
papers.summary: This paper describes the rational design of improved fluorogenic probes for CapV, a phospholipase effector in bacterial CBASS antiphage defense systems, because the commonly used resorufin butyrate substrate is hydrolyzed even by basal (unactivated) CapV and thus poorly distinguishes activation states. The authors also identify molecular determinants governing how the cyclic dinucleotide cGAMP binds to and activates CapV, providing a better toolkit for studying this widespread antiphage signaling pathway.

papers.title: Zinc peroxide-coated gold nanorods as the therapeutic adjuvants for photothermal enhanced chemodynamic therapy and metalloimmunotherapy against tumor.
papers.abstract: Traditional tumor therapies have limited efficacy, leading to a high mortality rate. Although immunotherapy holds considerable therapeutic promise, clinical immunotherapy for solid tumors only elicits durable responses in a minority of patients. This limitation is largely attributed to the highly immunosuppressive nature of the tumor microenvironment (TME). Notably, conventional chemodynamic therapy (CDT) is hampered by endogenous hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) shortage in tumor cells, and AZP compensates this defect via in-situ H2O2 self-supplementation to amplify hydroxyl radical generation.
papers.summary: This study develops zinc peroxide-coated gold nanorods (AZP) as a multifunctional therapeutic adjuvant for cancer treatment. The zinc peroxide coating self-supplies hydrogen peroxide within tumor cells, overcoming the typical shortage that limits chemodynamic therapy, while the gold nanorods enable photothermal therapy. Together these effects amplify hydroxyl radical generation and, through zinc release, stimulate metalloimmunotherapy to counteract the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment.

papers.title: Diversification and functional expansion of archaeal T4F machineries.
papers.abstract: Archaea have several cell surface structures belonging to the type 4 filament (T4F) superfamily. All share a minimal core assembly system consisting of an ATPase, a platform protein, a filament-forming protein, and a class III signal peptidase. Here, we generated novel MacSyFinder2 models to identify and classify archaeal T4F systems. Our analysis revealed a vast diversity of archaeal T4F, with many organisms harboring one or more assembly machineries. Structure-based phylogenetic analysis showed that the variable N-terminal domain of T4F-related ATPases mirrors the subsystem clustering, indic
papers.summary: The authors built new MacSyFinder2 models to systematically identify and classify type 4 filament (T4F) assembly systems across archaeal genomes. They found that archaea harbor a much greater diversity of T4F machineries than previously recognized, with many organisms carrying multiple systems, and that structure-based phylogenetics of the variable N-terminal domain of T4F ATPases recapitulates subsystem clustering. This work expands the known functional repertoire of archaeal cell surface structures and provides a classification framework for future studies.

papers.title: From GROMACS Molecular Dynamics Simulations to Electronic Absorption Spectra: A Tutorial for Small Molecules in Organic Solvents.
papers.abstract: Classical molecular dynamics is a theoretical method useful for investigating noncovalent intermolecular interactions and conformational flexibility, enabling the simulation of processes such as aggregation/dissolution and adsorption. Molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry are increasingly introduced in chemistry curricula, yet students may encounter difficulties when translating theoretical concepts into robust simulation protocols, particularly outside biomolecular systems. Here, we present a tutorial designed to guide students through the preparation, execution, and analysis of the simula
papers.summary: This tutorial guides students through a complete workflow that starts with preparing and running classical molecular dynamics simulations in GROMACS for small organic molecules in solvent, then uses the resulting configurations to compute electronic absorption spectra via quantum chemistry. It addresses a gap in chemistry curricula by showing how to translate theoretical concepts into a robust, reproducible simulation protocol outside biomolecular systems. The paper is pedagogical rather than presenting new scientific findings.

papers.title: On the binding of cell-adhesive proteins vitronectin, fibronectin and laminin to agarose hydrogel.
papers.abstract: Protein binding at hydrogel interfaces is a key process in biomaterials surface science, governing the biochemical response of cells. Here, we investigate the binding behavior of three cell-adhesive proteins with distinct molecular weights, namely, vitronectin, fibronectin, and laminin on a hydrogel network composed of a low-hydrophobic agarose. Binding kinetics was evaluated through a solution-depletion method. Using destabilizing agents such as the chaotropic salt magnesium perchlorate, Mg(ClO4)2, or the non-ionic surfactant Tween 20, our results show that binding is driven by hydrophobic ef
papers.summary: This study examines how three cell-adhesive proteins (vitronectin, fibronectin, and laminin) bind to agarose hydrogels, using solution-depletion kinetics and destabilizing agents (chaotropic salt, non-ionic surfactant). The results indicate that binding is driven by hydrophobic interactions, with protein molecular weight influencing the binding behavior. The work provides insight into protein-hydrogel interfacial interactions relevant to biomaterial design.

papers.title: Accelerating the discovery of nanoporous gas separation materials via Coulomb-enhanced classical density functional theory.
papers.abstract: The design of advanced nanoporous materials for gas separations, such as carbon capture and alkyne purification, is increasingly driven by high-throughput screening. However, the accurate description of electrostatic interactions in porous frameworks remains challenging and can introduce sizable deviations between predicted and experimental performance, thereby hindering rational materials design. To address this gap, we present a computational framework, compatible with standard force fields under appropriate charge assignments, that explicitly incorporates a point-charge model to capture ads
papers.summary: The authors present a computational framework that enhances classical density functional theory with an explicit point-charge model to better capture electrostatic interactions in nanoporous materials for gas separations. This approach aims to reduce discrepancies between predicted and experimental performance in high-throughput screening for applications like carbon capture and alkyne purification. The method is compatible with standard force fields under appropriate charge assignments, potentially accelerating the discovery of improved gas separation materials.

papers.title: Structural insights into the ligand modulation of MRGPRX4 conformational plasticity.
papers.abstract: Chronic pruritus is a debilitating condition with limited treatment options, particularly in cholestatic liver diseases, where bile acid dysregulation is a known trigger. Although Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor X4 (MRGPRX4) has recently been identified as a key mediator of bile acid-induced pruritus, the structural mechanisms underlying its inhibition remain poorly understood, hindering the development of therapeutic antagonists. Here, we report the cryo-electron microscopy structures of MRGPRX4 in three distinct states: agonist-bound state, antagonist-bound state, and apo state. Our s
papers.summary: This study presents cryo-EM structures of the itch receptor MRGPRX4 in agonist-bound, antagonist-bound, and apo states, revealing how ligand binding reshapes the receptor's conformation. These structural snapshots clarify the mechanism by which bile acids activate MRGPRX4 to trigger chronic itch in cholestatic liver disease and provide a template for designing antagonist drugs. The work directly supports structure-guided development of new antipruritic therapies.

papers.title: Design of ancestral protein-glutaminase with improved thermal stability.
papers.abstract: Protein-glutaminase (PG) from Chryseobacterium proteolyticum is an industrially valuable enzyme for protein deamidation; however, its application is limited because of insufficient thermal stability. Previous rational design studies have enhanced the thermostability of PG but often required labor-intensive, stepwise optimization. In this study, ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR) was used to engineer thermostable PG variants in a single design step. Eight ancestral PGs were constructed, all of which exhibited enhanced thermal stability compared with that of the wild type. The most stable v
papers.summary: Researchers used ancestral sequence reconstruction to resurrect eight ancestral versions of protein-glutaminase from Chryseobacterium proteolyticum, an industrially useful enzyme limited by poor heat stability. All eight ancestral variants were more thermostable than the wild-type enzyme, with the most stable one outperforming it substantially, showing that ASR can deliver thermostable enzymes in a single design step rather than through laborious stepwise rational design.

papers.title: Protein interactions with small molecules, peptides and proteins share residue cluster classes.
papers.abstract: Macromolecular interactions with small molecules, peptides, and proteins are fundamental to cellular function. Despite intensive efforts to identify small-molecule modulators of protein-protein interactions (PPIs), successfully targeted interfaces remain rare, reinforcing the premise that binding sites across these molecular scale regimes possess distinct structural architectures. We previously demonstrated that the densest topological regions of protein structures, categorized as a collection of Residue Cluster Classes (cRCC), can effectively classify global protein folds and PPI. Here, we le
papers.summary: The authors extend their Residue Cluster Classes (cRCC) framework to compare binding sites across three molecular scales: small molecules, peptides, and proteins. They find that the structural architectures of these binding sites share common residue cluster classes rather than being fundamentally distinct, challenging the assumption that PPI interfaces are uniquely difficult to target. This suggests that insights from small-molecule binding sites may transfer to peptide and protein interaction interfaces.

papers.title: Coupled effects of molecular weight and grafting density on protein adsorption in phosphorylcholine-based zwitterionic brushes.
papers.abstract: Zwitterionic polymer brushes are widely used to suppress nonspecific protein adsorption, yet their performance depends jointly on molecular weight and grafting density. Rational design remains difficult because these parameters are often examined separately or represented by a single conformational descriptor. Here, bovine serum albumin adsorption was systematically investigated across 22 poly(2-methacryloyloxyethyl phosphorylcholine) brush states prepared using a polydopamine-mediated grafting-to method that enabled systematic variation of molecular weight and grafting density. Quartz crystal
papers.journal: Journal of colloid and interface science
papers.summary: This study systematically varied both molecular weight and grafting density of zwitterionic phosphorylcholine polymer brushes across 22 states to examine how these coupled parameters affect nonspecific protein adsorption. The authors found that performance depends jointly on both parameters rather than on a single conformational descriptor, providing a framework for rational design of antifouling surfaces.

papers.title: Structure-Based Drug Design of Quinoline CYP8B1 Inhibitors for the Potential Treatment of Metabolic Disease.
papers.abstract: CYP8B1 has been identified as a potential target for the treatment of metabolic diseases, such as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and type 2 diabetes (T2D). CYP8B1 enzyme inhibitor 1 was discovered from a high-throughput screen of our compound collection; however, its poor metabolic stability prevented further in vivo evaluation. Leveraging structure-based drug design, metabolite identification and metabolic stability-guided DMPK optimization, and library synthesis to rapidly expand SAR, we identified compound 9 with substantially improved DMPK properties. Compound 9 showed robust in
papers.summary: The authors used structure-based drug design to optimize a quinoline-based inhibitor of CYP8B1, a target for metabolic diseases like NAFLD and type 2 diabetes. Starting from a high-throughput screening hit with poor metabolic stability, they identified metabolites and used DMPK-guided optimization to develop compound 9, which shows substantially improved drug-like properties and robust in vivo activity.

papers.title: Enhancing the Activity of Ribokinase from Thermus sp. 2.9 Through Rational Design for the Cascade Synthesis of Modified Nucleotides and Nucleosides.
papers.abstract: The pursuit of efficient approaches for the production of promising antiviral and cytostatic pharmaceuticals is a crucial direction in medical biotechnology, especially after the COVID-19 pandemic. Modified nucleosides and nucleotides represent a highly promising class of chemicals for the development of drugs against cancer and viral infections. Being an alternative to traditional chemical synthesis, cascades of nucleic exchange enzymes offer single-step synthesis of such compounds with exceptional stereo- and regioselectivity. Furthermore, employing thermostable enzymes for such cascades off
papers.summary: The authors used rational protein design to engineer a more active thermostable ribokinase from Thermus sp. 2.9, aiming to improve enzymatic cascade synthesis of modified nucleosides and nucleotides for antiviral and anticancer drug production. The engineered enzyme is intended to enable more efficient single-step, stereoselective synthesis of these compounds as an alternative to traditional chemical routes.

papers.title: Benzothiazole-Derived Compounds as Potential Drugs for the Treatment of Type 2 Diabetes: A Descriptive Review.
papers.abstract: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is a multifactorial metabolic disease in which hyperglycemia coexists with insulin resistance, β-cell dysfunction, dyslipidemia, and progressive microvascular and macrovascular complications. The structural versatility of the benzothiazole scaffold has enabled the development of a diverse array of preclinical compounds capable of modulating multiple diabetes-relevant targets. This review critically analyzes the available evidence on benzothiazole-derived compounds exhibiting antidiabetic or other diabetes-related pharmacological activities. No lower publication-date limit
papers.summary: This review surveys preclinical benzothiazole-derived compounds that show antidiabetic or diabetes-related pharmacological activity, covering multiple targets relevant to type 2 diabetes such as hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, and β-cell dysfunction. It catalogs the structural versatility of the benzothiazole scaffold and the range of diabetes-relevant mechanisms these compounds can modulate. The paper is a descriptive synthesis of preclinical evidence rather than new experimental data.

papers.title: Conformational Sampling of CPT1A Enables Dynamic Structure-Based Ligand Screening.
papers.abstract: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A (CPT1A) catalyzes a rate-limiting step in fatty acid β-oxidation and is a target for studies of metabolic disease and cancer. However, the structural dynamics of CPT1A remain poorly understood due to the lack of full-length structure. In this study, we employed an integrated computational approach combining molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, Markov state models (MSMs), and binding free energy calculations to elucidate the conformational landscape of human CPT1A. We performed an all-atom MD simulation of CPT1A embedded in a realistic outer mitochondrial membr
papers.summary: This study uses molecular dynamics simulations, Markov state models, and binding free energy calculations to map the conformational landscape of full-length human CPT1A embedded in a mitochondrial membrane. The authors identify distinct conformational states that could be targeted for structure-based ligand screening, addressing the lack of experimental full-length structures for this metabolic enzyme.

papers.title: Rational Design and Delivery of Engineered Peptides: Toward a Unified Framework for Structure, Screening, and Application.
papers.abstract: This review presents a three-tiered engineering framework that systematically addresses these barriers. First, we survey chemical and sequence-based stabilization strategies, including lipidation, backbone N-methylation, and cyclization, that convert labile natural peptides into protease-resistant scaffolds. Second, moving beyond generic stabilization, we dissect the rational design of effector-inhibitory peptides, with particular emphasis on disulfide bond topology engineering as a powerful means to lock binding-competent conformations, alongside structure-guided interface optimization. Third
papers.summary: This review proposes a three-tiered framework for engineering therapeutic peptides, covering chemical stabilization strategies (lipidation, N-methylation, cyclization) to improve protease resistance, rational design of effector-inhibitory peptides with emphasis on disulfide topology engineering, and downstream screening and delivery considerations. It aims to unify structure-based design principles with practical application, though as a review it synthesizes existing approaches rather than presenting new experimental data.

papers.title: Design and Evaluation of Novel Peptides Targeting Protein Disulfide Isomerase as Antiplatelet Agents.
papers.abstract: Extracellular protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) is a critical mediator of thrombus formation and a promising target for novel antithrombotic therapies aiming to overcome the bleeding risks associated with current antiplatelet agents. This study aimed to design and evaluate novel, targeted peptide-based PDI inhibitors with a safe physiological profile. We utilized a bioinformatics-driven rational design approach, based on the evolutionary conservation of the PDI active site, to generate a library of 34 targeted peptides. The inhibitory mechanism and biological efficacy of the lead candidate, pe
papers.summary: The authors used evolutionary conservation of the PDI active site to rationally design a library of 34 peptides targeting extracellular protein disulfide isomerase, a mediator of thrombus formation. They identified and characterized a lead peptide inhibitor with a favorable safety profile, aiming to develop antithrombotic agents that avoid the bleeding risks of current antiplatelet drugs.

papers.title: Screening and identification of a novel umami peptide with in vitro anti-inflammatory potential from sea cucumber protein: Integration of flavoromics, bioinformatic prediction, molecular simulation and experimental validation.
papers.abstract: Sea cucumber protein was sequentially hydrolyzed with pepsin, trypsin, and enterokinase to obtain peptides with desirable taste characteristics and immunomodulatory potential. Multi-scale characterization, flavoromics, peptidomics, bioinformatic screening, molecular simulations, and cellular assays were employed to investigate the structural changes, flavor remodeling, and bioactivity of the resulting hydrolysates. Results showed that hydrolysis disrupted the compact protein structure, induced conformational unfolding, and yielded short peptides (0.5-1.5 kDa) with enhanced hydrophilicity and p
papers.summary: This study used a multi-step enzymatic hydrolysis of sea cucumber protein to generate short peptides (0.5–1.5 kDa) with improved taste and immunomodulatory properties. By combining flavoromics, peptidomics, bioinformatic screening, molecular simulations, and cell assays, the authors identified a novel umami peptide with in vitro anti-inflammatory activity. The work demonstrates an integrated pipeline for discovering bioactive food-derived peptides with dual flavor and health benefits.

papers.title: Imidazo[1,2-b]Pyrazole-1,2,4-oxadiazole Linked 1,2,3-Triazoles: Synthesis, Antibacterial, Biofilm, and In Silico Studies.
papers.abstract: The growing incidence of bacterial resistance, especially in gram-positive infections, emphasizes how urgently new antibacterial medicines must be developed. This study presents the rational design and synthesis of a series of fused imidazo[1,2-b]pyrazole-1,2,4-oxadiazole-1,2,3-triazole hybrids (8a-8n) employing a multi-step synthetic approach that includes oxidative cyclisation, amidoxime formation, Vilsmeier-mediated cyclodehydration, and Cu(I)-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC). The synthesized compounds were assessed for their in vitro antibacterial efficacy against Bacillus subt
papers.summary: The authors synthesized a series of 14 fused imidazo[1,2-b]pyrazole-1,2,4-oxadiazole-1,2,3-triazole hybrid compounds using a multi-step route including CuAAC click chemistry, then tested them for antibacterial activity against Bacillus subtilis and other strains. The study also evaluated biofilm inhibition and performed in silico docking to rationalize the observed activity. The work is a medicinal chemistry structure-activity exploration aimed at developing new agents against gram-positive bacterial infections.

papers.title: Potential molecular links between triclosan exposure and osteoarthritis: An integrative systems toxicology study.
papers.abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a chronic disease affecting the entire joint, influenced by a combination of inflammatory, metabolic, immune, and environmental factors. Triclosan (TCS), a commonly used antimicrobial compound, has been linked to oxidative and immune disturbances; however, its molecular relevance to OA remains to be elucidated. This study integrated network toxicology, bulk transcriptomics, cross-cohort machine learning prioritization, immune infiltration analysis, single-cell transcriptomic analysis, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and primary chondrocyte experiments.
papers.summary: This study integrates network toxicology, bulk and single-cell transcriptomics, machine learning, and molecular simulations to identify potential molecular links between triclosan exposure and osteoarthritis. The authors prioritize candidate genes across cohorts, analyze immune infiltration, and validate findings with primary chondrocyte experiments, suggesting triclosan may contribute to OA through oxidative and immune-related pathways.

papers.title: Network pharmacology-driven identification of PTP1β and rational design of simufilam-based allosteric inhibitors for neuroprotection in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that predominantly affects elderly people and is characterized by cognitive decline and dementia. Protein tyrosine phosphatase-1B (PTP1B) is known to modulate pro-inflammatory mediators, and its overexpression in the brain has been implicated in AD-associated neuroinflammation. This study explores the mechanism of A20, A26, and co-crystal-designed compound targeting non-competitive allosteric PTP1B enzyme inhibition for AD therapy using network pharmacology and computational studies. Protein-protein interaction was designed f
papers.summary: This study uses network pharmacology and computational docking to identify PTP1B as a target for Alzheimer's disease neuroinflammation and to design simufilam-based allosteric inhibitors. The authors propose that non-competitive allosteric inhibition of PTP1B by these compounds could reduce pro-inflammatory signaling and provide neuroprotection. The work is largely computational and requires experimental validation.

papers.title: Clodronate and trehalose exhibit a paradoxical antagonistic interaction that suppresses proliferation of canine mammary tumour cells.
papers.abstract: Clodronate and trehalose are known to modulate metabolic and autophagy-related pathways, respectively, yet their combined effects on tumour cell proliferation remain poorly understood. This study investigated the individual and combined effects of these compounds on the canine mammary tumour cell line CMT-U27 and explored underlying mechanisms using network pharmacology. Cell proliferation was assessed following treatment with clodronate, trehalose, and their combination across a range of concentrations. Growth rate analysis and Bliss independence modelling were used to evaluate drug interacti
papers.summary: This study tested clodronate and trehalose, alone and in combination, on a canine mammary tumour cell line. Unexpectedly, the two compounds antagonized each other, suppressing tumour cell proliferation less than expected from their individual effects, and network pharmacology was used to explore the underlying mechanisms. The work highlights a paradoxical drug interaction relevant to veterinary oncology.

papers.title: A single amino acid mutation alters substrate specificity towards l-glucose in a bacterial l-galactose dehydrogenase.
papers.abstract: Structure-based mutagenesis was performed to modify the substrate specificity of bacterial l-galactose dehydrogenase from Luteolibacter sp. strain LG18, which also exhibits intrinsic l-glucose dehydrogenase activity. Based on previously reported crystal structures of the enzyme in ternary complex with l-galactose or l-glucose and NADP+, an M212Q mutant was generated and found to exhibit a pronounced preference for l-glucose. Kinetic analysis showed that the M212Q mutant displayed an approximately 20-fold higher k cat/K M value for l-glucose than for l-galactose. To elucidate the structural bas
papers.summary: Researchers used structure-based mutagenesis to alter the substrate specificity of a bacterial L-galactose dehydrogenase that also has intrinsic L-glucose dehydrogenase activity. The single M212Q mutation shifted the enzyme's preference toward L-glucose, yielding a ~20-fold higher catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM) for L-glucose over L-galactose. This demonstrates that a single amino acid change can effectively reprogram sugar substrate specificity in this enzyme family.

papers.title: Rational structure-guided identification of a Bcl-2-targeting peptide with antiproliferative effects on colorectal cancer cells.
papers.abstract: Bcl-2 is critical for tumour survival and serves as a promising anticancer drug target. Herein, a series of novel Bcl-2-targeted peptides were identified through structure-based virtual screening and systematic biological validation. Four candidate peptides were selected from the peptide library. MST results demonstrated that Peptide 1 exhibited the strongest apparent binding affinity towards Bcl-2 (Kd = 0.51 ± 0.03 μM), superior to VS-9 and other screened peptides. Molecular dynamics simulation, free energy landscape analysis, and MM/GBSA calculation further supported the predicted conformati
papers.journal: Journal of enzyme inhibition and medicinal chemistry
papers.summary: The authors used structure-based virtual screening to identify peptides that bind Bcl-2, a key anti-apoptotic protein in cancer, then validated the top candidates experimentally. Peptide 1 showed the strongest binding affinity (Kd ≈ 0.51 μM), and molecular dynamics and free energy calculations supported the predicted binding mode. The peptide also exhibited antiproliferative effects on colorectal cancer cells, suggesting a potential starting point for Bcl-2-targeting anticancer therapeutics.

papers.title: In Silico Design and Immunogenicity Evaluation of a Multiepitope Vaccine Candidate Against Leishmania tropica in BALB/c Mice.
papers.abstract: Cutaneous leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania tropica remains a major neglected parasitic disease with limited therapeutic options and frequent treatment failure, highlighting the urgent need for effective vaccine-based interventions. Multiepitope vaccine (MEV) strategies provide a rational and targeted approach to induce defined cellular and humoral immune responses against Leishmania infection.
papers.summary: This study reports the computational design of a multiepitope vaccine candidate against Leishmania tropica, the parasite causing cutaneous leishmaniasis, by selecting immunogenic epitopes and evaluating their predicted ability to stimulate cellular and humoral immunity. The candidate was then tested in BALB/c mice to assess immunogenicity, providing preliminary in vivo support for the in silico design. The work aims to address the limited therapeutic options for this neglected parasitic disease by offering a rationally designed vaccine approach.

papers.title: Integrated immunoreactivity analysis of MHC-I epitopes derived from the Marburg virus glycoprotein.
papers.abstract: Marburg virus (MARV) is a hemorrhagic fever virus, and its glycoprotein (GP) represents an important target for vaccine research. MHC class I (MHC-I)-restricted T cell epitopes are critical for inducing cytotoxic CD8+ T cell responses. In this study, we aimed to identify MHC-I-restricted T cell epitopes derived from the MARV Angola strain GP through an integrated bioinformatics and experimental approach.
papers.summary: This study combines bioinformatics predictions with experimental validation to identify MHC class I-restricted T cell epitopes from the Marburg virus glycoprotein (Angola strain). The work provides a set of candidate epitopes that could inform CD8+ T cell-based vaccine design against Marburg virus.

papers.title: Unlocking the molecular mechanisms of bamboo-based remediation of hazardous contaminants: macromolecular interactions, transport pathways, and predictive approaches.
papers.abstract: Bamboo presents an unusual combination of rapid biomass production and diverse molecular mechanisms for capturing, transforming, and sequestering hazardous contaminants. However, the existing investigations have predominantly focused on bulk removal efficiencies and tissue-level accumulation profiles, whereas the molecular determinants governing these processes remain critically underexplored. This review systematically synthesizes the structure-function relationships of key bamboo-derived macromolecules including cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, membrane transport proteins such as heavy meta
papers.summary: This review synthesizes how bamboo-derived macromolecules—cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, and membrane transport proteins—capture, transform, and sequester hazardous contaminants, moving beyond bulk removal metrics to molecular structure-function relationships. It also discusses transport pathways and predictive modeling approaches for bamboo-based phytoremediation. The work highlights a gap: molecular determinants of contaminant handling in bamboo remain underexplored despite the plant's rapid biomass production.

papers.title: Engineering a hemoglobin variant with enhanced stability and oxygen affinity using a protein language model.
papers.abstract: Engineered hemoglobin variants offer therapeutic promise for artificial blood substitutes and oxygen therapeutics, but rational design is constrained by protein stability and heme-binding. Protein language models (pLMs) predict mutation fitness, yet their integration with biophysical validation remains limited.
papers.summary: The authors use a protein language model to design hemoglobin variants with improved stability and oxygen affinity, then validate the designs biophysically. This demonstrates how pLM-guided mutation prediction can be combined with experimental screening to engineer oxygen-carrying proteins for therapeutic use.

papers.title: Identification of psoriasis-associated hub genes by integrated transcriptomics and machine learning.
papers.abstract: This study aims to systematically identify key hub genes in psoriasis pathogenesis through the integration of bioinformatics, machine learning and experimental validation methods. Four psoriasis microarray datasets were retrieved from the GEO database, with differentially expressed genes identified through comparative analysis. A dual machine learning approach screened core hub genes, whose expression levels and diagnostic efficacy were validated in an independent cohort. CIBERSORT was employed for immune cell infiltration analysis, whilst a multi-database approach constructed an mRNA-miRNA-ln
papers.summary: This study integrates four public psoriasis microarray datasets with differential expression analysis and two machine-learning feature-selection methods to identify hub genes involved in psoriasis pathogenesis. Candidate genes were validated in an independent cohort for expression and diagnostic performance, and immune cell infiltration was profiled with CIBERSORT alongside an mRNA-miRNA-lncRNA regulatory network. The work nominates candidate biomarkers and immune-cell signatures for psoriasis, though the findings are computational and require broader experimental confirmation.

papers.title: Molecular characterization and pathogenicity stratification of YWHAG missense variants in developmental and epileptic encephalopathy.
papers.abstract: Variants in YWHAG cause severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) with early-onset seizures. Rapid and precise clinical classification of its missense variants presents a substantial challenge. This study sought to explore YWHAG spatiotemporal expression-pathogenicity correlation and reliable pathogenicity indicators for its variants to promote clinical genetic diagnosis.
papers.summary: This study investigates missense variants in the YWHAG gene, which cause a severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with early-onset seizures. The authors examine the spatiotemporal expression pattern of YWHAG and its correlation with variant pathogenicity, aiming to identify reliable indicators for classifying variants and improving clinical genetic diagnosis.

papers.title: An entosis-informed prognostic index for survival stratification and molecular characterization in lung adenocarcinoma.
papers.abstract: Entosis is an actomyosin-dependent cell-in-cell process that may culminate in lysosome-mediated entotic cell death and is implicated in tumor evolution. Its clinical relevance in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) remains unclear.
papers.journal: Frontiers in cell and developmental biology
papers.summary: This study constructs a prognostic index for lung adenocarcinoma based on genes related to entosis, a cell-in-cell process implicated in tumor evolution. The index is used to stratify patients by survival and to characterize the molecular features associated with different risk groups. It suggests that entosis-related gene signatures may have clinical utility in LUAD prognosis.

papers.title: MEMO1-ERα interaction may occur independent of Y537 phosphorylation which differs from MEMO1-ErbB2 binding.
papers.abstract: MEMO1 is a protein implicated in cancer-associated signaling through interactions with other proteins, including estrogen receptor α (ERα). We used fluorescence polarization, molecular dynamics simulations, and protein pull-down assays to characterize the interaction between MEMO1 and ERα. MEMO1 bound to an ERα peptide containing phosphorylated Y537 but unexpectedly showed comparable affinity for the non-phosphorylated peptide. Computational modeling identified distinct binding modes and suggested contributions from MEMO1 residues. Pull-down experiments confirmed interaction between MEMO1 and
papers.summary: This study characterizes how the protein MEMO1 binds to estrogen receptor alpha (ERα), a key driver of breast cancer. Contrary to expectation, MEMO1 bound equally well to ERα peptides whether or not tyrosine 537 was phosphorylated, suggesting the interaction does not depend on this modification and differs from MEMO1's known ErbB2 binding mode. Computational modeling and pull-down assays support distinct binding modes involving specific MEMO1 residues.

papers.title: Targeting Muscle-Specific E3 Ligases in Cancer Cachexia Through Structure-Based Virtual Screening of Small-Molecule Inhibitors.
papers.abstract: Cachexia is a multifactorial metabolic syndrome characterized by severe skeletal muscle loss that cannot be reversed by nutritional support. Common in cancer and other chronic diseases, it significantly increases morbidity and mortality. Muscle wasting is primarily driven by activation of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway through the E3 ubiquitin ligases MuRF1 and Atrogin-1, which promote protein degradation and muscle atrophy. This study used computational modeling and docking to identify small-molecule inhibitors targeting these ligases, including repurposed drugs with anti-cachectic potentia
papers.summary: This study uses computational modeling and molecular docking to screen small molecules, including repurposed drugs, for their ability to inhibit the muscle-specific E3 ubiquitin ligases MuRF1 and Atrogin-1, which drive muscle protein degradation in cancer cachexia. The work identifies candidate inhibitors with potential anti-cachectic activity, though experimental validation is not reported. It provides a starting point for developing targeted therapies against muscle wasting.

papers.title: Potential Molecular Links Between Benzophenone-3 and Breast Cancer: Network Toxicology, Machine Learning, Molecular Modeling, and Gene Expression Validation.
papers.abstract: Benzophenone-3 (BP-3) is a widely used ultraviolet filter with potential carcinogenic concern, but its molecular link with breast cancer remains unclear. This study aimed to identify candidate targets and potential molecular links between BP-3 and breast cancer using toxicological prediction, machine learning, molecular modeling, and gene expression analysis.
papers.summary: This study integrates network toxicology, machine learning, molecular docking, and gene expression validation to identify candidate molecular targets linking the UV filter benzophenone-3 (BP-3) to breast cancer. The authors propose potential target proteins and pathways through which BP-3 exposure might contribute to breast carcinogenesis, offering hypotheses for future experimental work. The findings are computational and correlative, requiring further validation.

papers.title: Mechanism of luteolin in treating chronic heart failure by regulating HIF-1 signaling pathway-mediated mitochondrial damage to inhibit cardiomyocyte apoptosis.
papers.abstract: Chronic heart failure (CHF) is a systemic cardiovascular disease characterized by an extremely poor prognosis. Luteolin demonstrates promising therapeutic potential in the prevention and management of CHF. This study aims to explore the mechanism by which luteolin ameliorates CHF through mitigating mitochondrial damage and inhibiting cardiomyocyte apoptosis, using bioinformatics analysis combined with in vitro and in vivo experiments.
papers.journal: Frontiers in cell and developmental biology
papers.summary: This study investigates how luteolin, a plant flavonoid, protects against chronic heart failure by targeting the HIF-1 signaling pathway. Using bioinformatics plus in vitro and in vivo experiments, the authors show that luteolin reduces mitochondrial damage and cardiomyocyte apoptosis, suggesting HIF-1-mediated mitochondrial protection as a therapeutic mechanism. The work supports luteolin as a candidate natural compound for heart failure treatment.

papers.title: Advances and applications of engineered protein therapeutics and their role in precision medicine.
papers.abstract: Proteins are a vital class of biomolecules. They play essential roles in biological processes, including building cellular structures, forming cellular channels and receptors, catalyzing biological reactions, transporting molecules, and contributing to immune defense mechanisms. Advances in protein engineering have enabled the genetic modification of naturally occurring proteins, using recombinant deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) technology, leading to the development of therapeutic proteins with enhanced specificity, stability, and clinical performance. Despite the rapid growth of engineered biolo
papers.summary: This review surveys how protein engineering, powered by recombinant DNA technology, has produced therapeutic proteins with improved specificity, stability, and clinical performance. It discusses the expanding range of engineered biologics and their integration into precision medicine strategies. The abstract is truncated, so specific findings beyond this overview are not available.

papers.title: Structure-based discovery of a novel Granzyme A (GZMA) inhibitor for autism spectrum disorder through integrative transcriptomics, virtual screening, and long-timescale molecular dynamics simulations.
papers.abstract: Granzyme A (GZMA) is a trypsin-like serine protease expressed in cytotoxic lymphocytes that cleaves gasdermin B (GSDMB) to release a pore-forming N-terminal fragment, thereby inducing pyroptosis, a lytic and pro-inflammatory form of programmed cell death. This pathway has been implicated in immune dysregulation reported in a subset of individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). In this study, we reanalyzed the peripheral blood transcriptome dataset GSE26415 using an integrative computational framework comprising outlier-aware quality control, differential expression analysis, functional e
papers.summary: The authors reanalyzed a peripheral blood transcriptome dataset from autism spectrum disorder (ASD) patients and identified Granzyme A (GZMA) as a potential therapeutic target linked to immune dysregulation and pyroptosis. Using virtual screening and long-timescale molecular dynamics simulations, they discovered a novel small-molecule inhibitor of GZMA. This work proposes a structure-based drug discovery strategy for a subset of ASD cases, though experimental validation is still needed.
